# VFD Pump Control Narrative: Template and P-1102 Example

## Two points to settle first

1. **Scope under batch control.** P-1102 gets its start, stop and speed commands from the batch system, so it is an ISA-88 control module. This narrative covers only device behavior: states, protection and abnormal handling. The phase logic belongs in the ISA-88 phase specification. That logic covers when to transfer, how much to transfer, and what to do when the phase holds. ISA-106 state tables still work well at device level, but do not try to use this document for unit procedures.
2. **Where the numbers live.** Your I/O list and alarm database hold ranges and alarm setpoints. They usually do not hold timers, speed clamps or watchdogs. The template refers to a **Setpoint List (SPL)** for these values. If you do not have one, add an SPL tab to the I/O list workbook. Otherwise each engineer will type values into the narrative prose.

---

**Ownership.** The command source is Program or Operator, as defined in R1 §{x}. Out of Service is a state, not an ownership.

**State table**

| State | Description | Entry permissives | Entry initiator | Allowed exits | Automation level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OUT OF SERVICE | Commands are blocked. Run command is off. | Run feedback off. Maintenance privilege. | Operator | STOPPED | Manual |
| STOPPED | Run command is off. Run feedback is off. | None | Automatic (end of SEQ-2, reset, or return from OOS) | STARTING, OUT OF SERVICE | — |

| RUNNING | Speed follows the reference within the SPL clamps. | SEQ-1 complete | Automatic | STOPPING, TRIPPED | Automatic |
| STOPPING | SEQ-2 runs. | None | Owner (stop command) or a non-latched interlock | STOPPED, TRIPPED | Automatic |
| TRIPPED | Run command is held off. A latched trip is active. | None | Automatic (latched cause) | STOPPED (reset), OUT OF SERVICE | Operator-prompted |

**Transitions**

| ID | From → To | Trigger | Initiator |
|---|---|---|---|
| TR-01 | STOPPED → STARTING | Start command, and all start permissives true | Owner |
| TR-02 | STARTING → RUNNING | SEQ-1 complete | Auto |
| TR-03 | STARTING/RUNNING → STOPPING | Stop command, or a non-latched interlock in R4 | Owner / Auto |
| TR-04 | STOPPING → STOPPED | SEQ-2 complete | Auto |
| TR-05 | Any running state → TRIPPED | Latched cause in R4, a SEQ failure, or an uncommanded stop | Auto |
| TR-06 | TRIPPED → STOPPED | Reset command, and all latched causes clear | Operator |
| TR-07 | STOPPED/TRIPPED → OUT OF SERVICE | OOS command | Operator (maintenance) |
| TR-08 | OUT OF SERVICE → STOPPED | Return-to-service command | Operator (maintenance) |

| ID | Requirement | Test |

| FR-{MOD}-012 | Every RUNNING state exit through STOPPING or TRIPPED sends a "stopped" status to {batch system} with the cause. | T |

## Notes for rolling this out across 120 modules

- **Lock the typical.** Most of the requirement text is the same for every pump. Keep the VFD-PUMP typical as a controlled document. Each pump narrative then records only the tags, the R4 rows, and the Section 11 deviations. One MOC on the typical then updates all pumps at the same time, and you avoid 120 copies drifting apart.
- **One FAT procedure per typical.** Write one FAT procedure per typical, with requirement IDs as test steps. Run it once per pump with the pump's tag table. The FR-ID scheme maps one-to-one to test steps.
- **Same skeleton for other module types.** On/off valves, modulating valves and agitators should follow the same skeleton: one state table, one SEQ table, and one parameter list per typical.
- **Engineering decisions.** I made several engineering decisions in the example: stop on batch comms loss, stop on bad PT-1102, and pressure prove at start. They are tracked as open items because process and operations must agree to them, not because they are unusual.
